newsitem.title: USA: UPS chairman, Teamsters president in last-ditch talks.
newsitem.headline: UPS chairman, Teamsters president in last-ditch talks.

text.p: United Parcel Service Chairman James Kelly and Teamsters President Ron Carey personally entered negotiations late Thursday in a last-ditch bid to avert a strike that threatened to cripple the nation's largest largest package carrier.
Carey held out hope that an agreement could be reached just before talks between the two sides began at the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service in downtown Washington DC.
"I am always optimistic and will continue to be so until 12 o'clock," Carey said, referring to a midnight deadline. "We're here to negotiate a contract, not a strike," he said.
Kelly, chairman and chief executive officer of UPS, declined comment before the talks began.

The adversaries got together briefly at the Washington Court Hotel, then left to settle down to serious talks at the National Mediation and Conciliation Service, said Brian Flores, national representative for the service.

"Time is getting short, there's only a few hours left," said John Calhoun Wells, head of the mediation service. "Both sides have agreed to my request to meet face to face. At this late stage, every step is like climbing a mountain."
The two sides are negotiating a new five-year contract to replace the existing one, which expires at midnight.
If the approximately 200,000 Teamsters strike UPS, more than 12 million packages destined for roughly 1.5 million U.S. customers a day will be stranded, along with others overseas.
The key issues in the negotiations are creation of more full-time jobs, an end to subcontracting, safety and health issues and pension issues, the union said.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said a senior adviser, Bruce Lindsey, had met with officials from both sides earlier Thursday, but an administration official said President Bill Clinton was not considering intervening.

Clinton intervened under the Railway Labour Act to end an American Airlines strike minutes after it began earlier this year. But to halt a UPS walkout, Clinton would have to use the cumbersome and time-consuming Taft-Hartley law, which has not been used since the 1950s, to order a mediation board to settle the dispute, the administration official said.
The company said earlier it had made its "last, best and final offer" Wednesday evening. The union rejected that offer.
If the strike takes place, Congress might be inclined to reconsider labour laws governing UPS, an analyst said.
The strike would idle approximately 200,000 Teamsters, two-thirds of UPS's work force. The two sides even disagreed on the number: The union said 185,000 and the company 214,000.

A stumbling block is the fate of part-timers at UPS, who make up more than half the firm's union membership. The company has offered to convert roughly 10 percent of the part-time employees, or 10,000, to full-time work over the five-year contract. The union says that is not enough.
The company also wants to break up the Teamsters pension fund, substituting a joint company-union fund that includes only UPS employees.

"We believe UPS dollars should directly benefit UPS employees, not support the Teamsters' pension funds," said company spokesman Ken Sternad. The company said that would improve pension benefits and might help it financially also.
A union spokesman had no comment on the pension issue.
But a union negotiator, who asked not to be identified, said if the company took over the pension plan employees would be unable to switch firms and preserve their pensions.

The contract would increase top pay for full-timers from $19.95 an hour to $21.45 by 2001, which the company says would be the highest in the industry. The lowest-paid part-time employees, who earn $8 an hour, would get $11 an hour by 2001.
If the strike occurs, the company's roughly 2,000 pilots who operate its 200 aircraft pledged to honour the picket line.

The company is the nation's largest package carrier, with 1996 revenues of $22.4 billion. It handles 3.15 billion parcels and documents shipped annually to more than 200 countries from 1,700 hubs and centres.
